opus-5.5.text:
Around 2019 to 2021 a lot of us, me included, were very excited. MoCo, SimCLR, then MAE. The feeling was that NLP had BERT and GPT, so vision would surely find its own self-supervised recipe, scale it up, and get the same leap. I spent years on this. But gradually I became pessimistic, for a few reasons.

The first is empirical. What made BERT and GPT special wasn't that they matched supervised pretraining. It was that when you scaled data and parameters, things kept getting better, and new capabilities appeared. With contrastive learning and MIM, we never saw that. You scale the model, scale the data, and the downstream gains are modest, then they saturate. Sometimes a bigger model trained this way is barely better than a smaller one. There was no "emergence." Without a good scaling curve, you don't have a GPT moment. You just have a better initialization.

The second reason is more fundamental, and it took me longer to accept. Language and images are very different kinds of data. Text is produced by humans. It is already a highly compressed, abstract representation of the world. When you predict the next token or a masked token, you are forced to model human thinking: semantics, reasoning, knowledge. In language, generation, understanding, and alignment with humans all collapse into one objective. That's why it works so beautifully.

Images are natural signals. They are just photons hitting a sensor. When you mask patches and reconstruct pixels, much of what the model learns is low-level statistics: texture, color, local continuity. You can do a very good job filling in a missing patch without really understanding what's in the scene. So the objective doesn't force semantics the way language modeling does. In vision, generation and understanding don't naturally unify.

Contrastive learning has a different problem. What it learns is basically invariance to the data augmentations you design: crops, color jitter, and so on. Those invariances are human priors. You're telling the model what should not matter, but you're not giving it a rich task that requires understanding. So it learns a good feature, but it's bounded by the augmentations. It isn't open-ended.

So my conclusion was that it's not about finding a cleverer pretext task. Pure vision, learned from static images, probably doesn't contain enough of the right signal to produce a GPT-like model on its own. The intelligence in GPT comes largely from language. For vision to have its moment, it probably has to be tied to language, or to interaction and action in the world, rather than learning from pixels alone. That shift in thinking is a big part of why I moved toward multimodal models.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling gains were modest and often saturated, but does not say contrastive methods that worked well on small models deteriorated at very large scale.

r002.rationale: It says contrastive learning learns invariance to designed augmentations such as crops and color jitter, which are human priors.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss negative samples or maximum entropy.

r004.rationale: It describes text as a compressed representation of the world, but does not identify compression of the training corpus as the mechanism through which NLP models acquire knowledge.

r005.rationale: It discusses masked-patch reconstruction and low-level statistics, but does not identify occlusion invariance as the learned property.

r006.rationale: It separately notes modest gains from scaling data and that contrastive learning is bounded by designed augmentations, but does not explain that more data adds limited information because the objective keeps teaching the same fixed invariance.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't one moment, it was a slow accumulation of disappointment. Around 2020, 2021, I was very excited. MoCo, SimCLR, then MAE came out, and we all thought, okay, this is it, vision is about to have its BERT moment. The recipe looked right: a self-supervised objective, scale up the data, scale up the model, and intelligence should emerge.

But then we actually did the scaling. We pushed data up, we pushed the model up, and the curves just... flattened. Not immediately, but much earlier than language models. With GPT, every time you added an order of magnitude of data, something qualitatively new showed up. With contrastive learning or masked image modeling, you'd get a few more points on ImageNet linear probing, a few more points on detection, and then it saturated. The pretrained model was a better initialization, but it was still just an initialization. It never became a "brain" that could do new things you didn't train it for.

So I started asking why, and I think the answer is in what the task actually forces the model to learn. In language, next-token prediction is almost a cheat code. To predict the next word well, you eventually have to model grammar, facts, reasoning, intention. The objective is simple, but the only way to drive the loss down is to understand more and more. The task has no ceiling.

Vision objectives aren't like that. Take masked image modeling. You mask out patches and ask the model to reconstruct pixels. Most of that reconstruction can be done with local texture, color continuity, low-level statistics. Once the model learns those, the loss is already pretty low, and there's very little gradient pushing it toward semantics. The task has a ceiling, and the ceiling is low. Contrastive learning has a different problem. You're defining what "the same" means through augmentations: crop, flip, color jitter. So you're hand-coding the invariances, and the model can only learn what your augmentations allow. It's a bit like writing the rules of the world by hand and then being surprised the model only knows those rules.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that these methods are essentially learning from images alone, with no "answer" in the data. Text is special because it's human-generated, it's already compressed, already carries intention and causality. A raw image is a sensor reading. There's no reason a pile of sensor readings should contain the same density of knowledge. So when we saw the scaling fail, the honest conclusion was not "we need a better trick," but that the whole paradigm, pure vision self-supervision as the road to a GPT moment, was probably a dead end. That's when I started thinking the path for vision has to go through language, or at least through something that supplies the supervision text naturally provides.

r001.rationale: It says scaling made performance curves flatten and saturate, not that contrastive methods deteriorated on very large models.

r002.rationale: It says contrastive learning defines sameness through hand-coded augmentations such as crops, flips, and color jitter, which determine the invariances learned.

r003.rationale: It does not mention negative samples or interpret them as a maximum-entropy regularizer.

r004.rationale: It calls text already compressed and rich in intention and causality, but does not describe corpus compression as the mechanism by which NLP models acquire knowledge.

r005.rationale: It discusses reconstructing masked patches, but does not identify occlusion invariance as what masked image modeling learns.

r006.rationale: It separately describes scaling saturation and augmentation-defined invariances, without explaining that more data adds limited information because the objective keeps teaching the same fixed invariance.

astra-6.text:
I became skeptical because there was a gap between learning a useful visual representation and learning something that could support a broad range of tasks. Contrastive learning and masked image modeling clearly helped with the first. But I didn’t see a clear path from those objectives to the second.

With contrastive learning, a lot depends on how you construct positive pairs and choose augmentations. You’re effectively specifying which differences the model should ignore. That can be useful for recognition, but other tasks may need precisely the spatial or fine-grained information you’re teaching it to discard.

Masked image modeling has a different issue: reconstructing missing image content doesn’t necessarily require semantic understanding. A model can make progress by exploiting local texture and continuity. So a better reconstruction loss doesn’t automatically mean a more capable visual system.

The question for me was whether scaling these objectives would keep producing new capabilities, rather than just better initialization for supervised tasks. I wasn’t convinced that the objective, the data, and the downstream interface were aligned well enough to produce that kind of transition. That’s skepticism about the path—not a claim that these methods aren’t useful.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that contrastive methods deteriorated when scaled from small to very large models.

r002.rationale: It says chosen augmentations specify which differences the model should ignore, identifying them as the source of learned invariances.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss negative samples as a regularizer or connect them to maximum entropy.

r004.rationale: It does not describe NLP models acquiring knowledge through compression of the training corpus.

r005.rationale: It discusses masked image reconstruction and local texture, but does not identify occlusion invariance as what masked image modeling learns.

r006.rationale: It questions whether scaling the objectives will produce new capabilities, but does not say that more data provides limited information because the objective teaches the same fixed, manually specified invariance.

sol-6.1.text:
I became skeptical because there was a gap between learning a good visual representation and learning something that could become a general-purpose interface for vision.

Contrastive learning gives you a powerful way to organize images: two augmented views of the same image should have similar representations. But what the model learns depends heavily on the augmentations and on what you tell it to treat as equivalent. That can be useful for recognition, without necessarily preserving the spatial detail you need for other tasks.

Masked image modeling has a different issue. In language, predicting a missing word often requires understanding the sentence. In an image, neighboring pixels contain a lot of redundant information. A model can solve parts of the reconstruction problem using local appearance, without necessarily understanding the objects or their relationships. So a better reconstruction loss doesn’t automatically mean a more capable visual system.

Neither approach is useless—both can produce very strong features. But strong features alone don’t establish a BERT or GPT moment. The question is whether the pretraining objective, as you scale it, produces increasingly general capabilities that you can access and adapt easily. I didn’t see a clear reason to assume these objectives would make that leap.

r001.rationale: It says contrastive learning can produce strong features, but does not state that methods successful on small models deteriorate at very large scale.

r002.rationale: It says the representation depends heavily on augmentations and on what the method treats as equivalent, identifying augmentations as a source of learned invariances.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss negative samples or interpret them as a maximum-entropy regularizer.

r004.rationale: It does not describe NLP models acquiring knowledge by compressing their training corpus.

r005.rationale: It discusses masked image modeling as reconstruction from redundant local pixels, but does not identify occlusion invariance as what it learns.

r006.rationale: It notes that contrastive learning depends on augmentations, but does not explain that more data adds limited information when the objective teaches the same fixed manually specified invariance.
